email.job: Standalone Tuesday broadcast telling the full comparison story and connecting the decision standard to ELEVATE. Use one reply invitation, no audit CTA and no claim that this client belongs to ELEVATE.
email.body:
Building something new can make the next decision seem obvious. The page is ready, the team has done the work, and switching traffic over can look like the natural next step.

But the fact that we created an alternative doesn't settle whether it should replace what's already there.

**We owe our own work the same scrutiny we give the work a client brings to us.**

In that conversation, I also described changes we planned to make to our page. Once those updates were made, I said I would send it back so the client could review it again.

Our version was something we were prepared to keep working on, rather than something the client's advertising had to accommodate because we'd built it.

If you've invested in your wedding business's marketing, you want a team that understands the value of that investment. You're hiring us to contribute expertise, make recommendations and give you clear reasoning for the decisions we take with your ads.

That includes distinguishing between having a new page available and having a reason to change where couples go after clicking.

We can bring a strong recommendation and still be open to improving our contribution. Respect for your existing work belongs alongside confidence in what we create.

It's the kind of judgment we bring to ELEVATE, our full-service advertising management program. The value of having an advertising team includes how we evaluate our own work, not only what we deliver.
email.ending:
Reply to this email, and let's see what the right next step looks like.

Talk soon,
Whitney

reels.script:
We built a landing page for a client, and we didn't move all their ad traffic to it.

A little context. They already had pages in their advertising, and we'd created another option. But building that option didn't automatically answer the question of where we should send couples.

On the call, I explained why we were comparing our page with the existing pages instead of switching everything over. We wanted to understand how our version would convert before making that change.

And I also told the client we were going to make updates to our page and send it back so they could take another look.

I think that matters when you're trusting someone with your advertising. You're bringing us in to make thoughtful decisions for your business, and sometimes that means taking another look at something our own team created.

We can believe in the page we've built and still give the pages you already have a fair comparison. Those two things can exist together.

What I want you to feel is that we're looking after your advertising, including being willing to improve our contribution before asking it to take the place of yours.

caption.body:
You've already put thought into how couples discover your business and where they go to learn more. When you bring in an advertising partner, you want that investment to be understood as the team considers what to add or change.

In one client conversation, I explained a decision involving a landing page we'd created. We were comparing it with the pages already being used rather than directing every ad click to our version simply because we'd built it.

I also outlined updates we planned to make before bringing the page back to the client for another review. Our contribution was open to refinement, just like anything else in the advertising.

That's an important part of how I think about the responsibility we're taking on. A team can have a clear recommendation without assuming every new asset should immediately replace an existing one. The reasoning has to serve the wedding business, including the couples considering it.

You should be able to see that care in the decisions we make about our own work, as well as the work we inherit.

For a wedding business, a page is part of the path a couple takes from discovering you to making an inquiry. Choosing where to send that couple deserves more consideration than who created the newest option.

We discussed exactly that in a client call. Our team had built a landing page, but the decision was to compare it with the client's existing pages before making a complete switch. Whitney then described refinements we intended to make and a further opportunity for the client to review our version.

reader_fit.why: This owner already has advertising and a website worth building on, and wants thoughtful ongoing management.
reader_fit.buyer_statement: “Clients come to us because they are ready for ads. They want to amplify what is already working.”

card.why_selected: This is the clearest counter-expected decision of the week. It adds something specific to earlier data-led content: WIA's own deliverable doesn't get preference simply because WIA made it.
card.wia_in_action: Whitney described comparing WIA's new landing page with the client's existing pages instead of moving all traffic at once. She then named revisions WIA would make to its own page and send back for the client's review.
card.why_it_matters: A new page shouldn't automatically replace a useful part of a wedding business's advertising. Owners should know how their ads team makes that decision.
evidence_points: Whitney said WIA used a comparison because it didn't want to stop sending traffic to the existing pages and switch everything to its own page without knowing how it would convert. (10:13–10:35)
Whitney said WIA would revise imagery, mobile presentation and calls to action on its page, then send it back for Lauren to review. (10:52–11:03)
card.reader_takeaway: I want a team that respects what's already working, even when they built the alternative.
verify_before_publishing: Confirm permission to use an anonymous account of the page-comparison decision.

surprise_for_experienced_advertiser.reason: An owner may expect an agency's preferred page to become the default; WIA was willing to keep using the client's existing work while assessing its own.
